title: Can you structure these 12 public sector case questions in two minutes each?
description: 12 public sector case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Public sector prompts test whether you can define success without a profit number. Start each one with the objective. Give yourself two minutes per prompt, then open the model and look for what you missed.
body:
1. Should a city introduce a congestion charge?

Show a model structure
  • Objectives: Less traffic, cleaner air, revenue; Alternatives: parking, bus lanes, low-emission zone
  • Impact: Drivers, residents, businesses, public transport; Who gains and who loses
  • Economics: Set-up and running cost; Revenue and what it pays for
  • Implementation: Public and political support; Technology, enforcement, timing

Where to start: Objectives: the right charge depends on whether the goal is traffic, air or revenue.

The trap: Running straight to revenue without asking what the city wants to achieve.

2. A government wants 1 million more women in work within five years.

Show a model structure
  • Who and where: Which groups are out of work and why; Regions and sectors with the biggest gap
  • Barriers: Childcare cost and availability; Flexible hours, skills, transport
  • Levers: Childcare funding, tax and benefits; Employer incentives, training
  • Delivery: Cost per extra woman in work; How to measure progress

Where to start: Who is out of work and why: the barriers differ by group.

The trap: Listing policies without first segmenting who is out of work.

3. How would you increase organ donor registrations?

Show a model structure
  • Awareness: Who knows they can register; Campaigns, stories
  • Ease: Opt-out law (raises consent, not registrations); Sign-up with driving licences, GP visits, apps
  • Trust and family: Fears and myths; Families overruling consent
  • Measurement: Registrations vs actual donations; Which channel converts best

Where to start: Ease: default and channel choices move registrations more than campaigns.

The trap: Only proposing awareness campaigns.

4. A group of 20 schools has seen exam results fall for two years.

Show a model structure
  • Which schools and subjects: Spread of the fall; Which year groups
  • Teachers: Turnover, vacancies, supply staff; Experience and training
  • Students: Attendance, intake changes; Support for those falling behind
  • Curriculum and leadership: Curriculum changes, exam board; School leaders and their priorities

Where to start: Which schools: a group-wide fall and a fall in five schools need different answers.

The trap: Assuming a group-wide cause before checking where the fall is.

5. A hospital's 30-day readmission rate is twice the national average.

Show a model structure
  • Which patients: Condition, age, ward; Planned vs emergency
  • In hospital: Treatment, early discharge; Medication at discharge
  • After discharge: Follow-up appointments, community care; Patients' understanding of their care
  • Data: Coding and how readmissions are counted; Comparison with similar hospitals

Where to start: Which patients: readmissions usually cluster in a few conditions.

The trap: Keeping everyone in longer, which costs a lot and may not help.

6. Should a city council merge four small primary schools into two?

Show a model structure
  • Students and families: Travel distance, places available; Effect on results
  • Costs: Savings on buildings and staff; Building works and transport
  • Quality: Teacher recruitment, class sizes; Specialist teaching
  • Community: Support and opposition; Use of the empty sites

Where to start: Students and families: the council will be judged on access and results.

The trap: Making it a cost-saving exercise only.

7. How could a government help more women start businesses?

Show a model structure
  • Who and why not: Barriers by sector and region; Compare with men starting
  • Money: Access to loans and investors; Grants and guarantees
  • Skills and networks: Mentoring, role models; Accelerators
  • Practical barriers: Childcare, time; Benefits and tax rules

Where to start: Who and why not: find which barrier is biggest by sector; access to investor money is often the largest.

The trap: Running awareness campaigns only.

8. How can a city raise its household recycling rate from 35% to 50%?

Show a model structure
  • Collection: Bins, frequency, food waste; Flats vs houses
  • Households: Space for bins, convenience; Incentives, rules
  • Contamination: Wrong items in bins; Checks and feedback
  • Processing: What our plants can sort; Markets for recycled materials

Where to start: Collection: food waste collection is often the biggest single lever.

The trap: Running leaflet campaigns only.

9. How could a rural region double its tourism income in five years?

Show a model structure
  • More visitors: Which markets, transport links; Marketing and partnerships
  • Longer stays: Things to do, events; Accommodation supply
  • More spend: Food, experiences, local products; Higher-value visitors
  • Seasons: Off-season attractions; Conferences and groups

Where to start: Longer stays: overnight visitors spend several times more than day-trippers.

The trap: Chasing visitor numbers that bring traffic but little spend.

10. How could a council get more eligible children to take free school meals?

Show a model structure
  • Who is missing out: Eligible but not registered; Registered but not eating
  • Registration: Automatic enrolment from benefits data; Simpler forms
  • Take-up: Quality and choice of food; Stigma, payment systems
  • Delivery: Kitchen capacity, cost per meal; Funding

Where to start: Automatic enrolment: removes the biggest barrier.

The trap: Improving menus while many eligible families never register.

11. How can a city's libraries double the number of people using them?

Show a model structure
  • Who uses them and who doesn't: By age and area; Why non-users stay away
  • What we offer: Books and digital lending; Events, study space, services
  • Access: Opening hours, locations; Online and mobile
  • Partnerships: School partnerships, job centres, health; Community groups

Where to start: Who doesn't come and why: target the biggest missing groups.

The trap: Only buying more books.

12. How can a city get bus ridership back to pre-pandemic levels?

Show a model structure
  • Who stopped: Commuters, students, older people; Routes and times
  • Service: Frequency, reliability; Bus lanes, journey times
  • Price: Fares, passes, contactless capping; Discounts for groups
  • Perception: Safety, cleanliness; Information and apps

Where to start: Who stopped: commuters working from home need different offers.

The trap: Cutting fares for everyone before knowing who stopped.

Identify the people hidden by averages

For congestion charging, the question is not just whether traffic declines. Assess commuters with viable transport alternatives, workers whose shifts start before public transport runs, tradespeople who carry equipment, local retailers and residents. The welfare and fairness effects may differ substantially between these groups.

An illustrative £10 charge paid by 50,000 vehicles each weekday would raise £500,000 gross per day before exemptions, collection costs, changes in travel behaviour and enforcement. But maximising collections is not necessarily the policy goal; successful congestion reduction may cause revenue to decline.

Specify a baseline, counterfactual and measurable outcomes: journey time, air quality, accessibility, administration cost and distributional impact. A strong public-sector tree shows who gains, who pays and which objective has priority.
